source_title: Security Council Renews Mandate of United Nations Support Mission in Libya for One Year, Unanimously Adopting Resolution 2835 (2026) - UN Meetings Coverage and Press Releases
source_excerpt:
The Security Council today extended the mandate of the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL ) for one year until 31 October 2027, reiterating its full support for the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Libya and Head of the Mission, Hanna S. Tetteh, in her efforts to further an inclusive political process.
The 15-member organ adopted resolution 2835 (2026) (to be issued as document S/RES/2835 (2026) by a vote of 13 in favour to none against, with 2 abstentions (Greece, Russian Federation).
By its terms, the Council noted the Mission’s steps to implement the recommendations of the Strategic Review (contained in document S/2025/611 ) and encouraged it to continue: placing support to a political solution to the Libyan conflict at the core of UNSMIL’s mandate; establishing a more consistent presence across Libya, including targeted expansions in Benghazi, Sabha and Sirte while maintaining a cost-neutral realignment and within existing resources; and increasing engagement in eastern and southern Libya with key stakeholders to support reunification efforts.
By other terms, the Council requested the Mission, in its implementation of the Strategic Review’s recommendations, to explore all avenues to increase efficiency and redeploy existing resources, including by prioritizing and reconfiguring tasks and resources, as needed.
Also, by the text, the Council called on Libyan political institutions and key stakeholders to engage fully, transparently and in good faith, without preconditions and without delay, and make the compromises necessary to progress a Libyan-led and Libyan-owned, UNSMIL-facilitated negotiation to deliver free and fair, transparent and inclusive national presidential and parliamentary elections.
Recalling the measures specified in paragraph 4 of Council resolution 2174 (2014), the Council urged all Libyan stakeholders to take steps to reunify all institutions and support the formation of a unified Libyan Government, and it urged all Member States to fully respect Libya’s sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity and national unity, and refrain from external interference. The Council called upon all parties to take further steps to implement the 23 October 2020 ceasefire agreement in full, including the action plan for the withdrawal of mercenaries, foreign fighters and foreign forces agreed upon by the 5+5 Joint Military Commission in Geneva on 8 October 2021.
The United Kingdom’s representative thanked all Council members for their constructive engagement in negotiations, emphasizing that the mandate will strengthen UNSMIL’s ability to advance a Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process and give Special Representative of the Secretary-General Tetteh a mandate to continue advancing her political road map . She urged all parties to honour the commitments they have made to provide Libyans the democratic choice, economic opportunity and security they deserve.
The representative of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, also speaking for Liberia and Somalia, urged the international community’s concerted support. Echoing other speakers, he said any political road map facilitated by UNSMIL must remain strictly under the ownership of the Libyans themselves, while all national institutions, including military institutions and security units, must create the necessary conditions for holding credible elections that reflect the will of the Libyan people.
He further voiced support for UNSMIL presence in Benghazi and elsewhere to move forward the national reunification process, urging necessary financial and human resources to that end. Voicing deep concern over the illicit flows of weapons to Libya, he strongly condemned “blind attacks on civilians and essential infrastructure”. He reiterated the demand for the unconditional withdrawal of all foreign forces and all foreign fighters and mercenaries in line with the full implementation of the ceasefire of 23 August 2020. Further, he expressed concern at the continued erosion of the value of frozen Libyan assets.
“There is a lot at stake here”, underscored the United States delegate, noting “a historic opportunity” for Libya whose strategic coastline on the Mediterranean and access to European and African markets points to an enormous untapped commercial potential. “With unified leadership, security and the right investments, Libya could become and should become a booming centre of international commerce, energy, shipping, finance”, he stressed, noting his country’s unification initiatives that offer a path to that future.
Rebuking leaders who would rather enrich themselves at the Libyan people’s expense, he warned: “There will be consequences for that behaviour.” He voiced frustration with efforts to “insert distracting language” reaffirming the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development or the Sustainable Development Goals, which intrude upon national sovereignty. “The Security Council should be focused on preventing wars, keeping the peace, and delivering real results”, he emphasized.
The representative of Greece, Council President for October, speaking in her national capacity, also shared her perspective on the text. It was crucial to strengthen relevant language, she said, recalling the “so-called Türkiye-Libya memorandum on the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction” ratified on 20 October by Libya’s House of Representatives. Greece and Libya, as natural maritime neighbours with opposite coasts, are entitled under international law to delimit their respective maritime zones through an agreement. Türkiye and Libya do not have opposite or adjacent coasts yet have attempted to establish an artificial maritime boundary between them “as if the Greek islands lying between their coasts simply don’t exist”. “This MoU is a flagrant violation of the fundamental principles of the international law of the sea”, she stressed.
“Any agreement on maritime delimitation must respect the sovereignty of States”, echoed the representative of France, reaffirming his country’s commitment to international law and the law of the sea. He commended the United Kingdom for the inclusive negotiations, which made it possible to strike a balance in the text.
China’s delegate underscored that promoting the implementation of the agreement reached by the 4+4 Smaller Convening, a political dialogue group which brings together two representatives from each of Libya’s four main rival institutions, is an important task for UNSMIL in the next phase. At the same time, the Mission should step up communication with relevant parties in Libya and ensure broad support for the agreement. International partners should fully respect Libya’s sovereignty and independence and refrain from imposing external solutions and undue sanctions and pressures.
The Russian Federation’s representative, explaining his abstention from the vote, said the constructive proposals for the resolution were not all reflected in today’s text. The agreements reached through “the small format” are a significant step forward, but their implementation is a “long way off”, he pointed out. They should be polished and secure the support from all influential Libyan stakeholders, he said.
